case_name: CASE OF AZADLIQ NEWSPAPER v. AZERBAIJAN

assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicant newspaper was ordered by domestic courts to publish a retraction and pay AZN 30,000 in non-pecuniary damages to T.A. following the publication of an article accusing him of misappropriation (see paragraphs 13, 14, 17 and 19). This judicial order directly restricted the newspaper’s ability to express critical opinions about a public figure and thus constituted an interference with its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference was grounded in domestic law, specifically Article 23 of the Civil Code of Azerbaijan, which provides for the protection of honour, dignity and business reputation and establishes civil liability for dissemination of harmful information (see paragraph 22). The defamation proceedings against the applicant newspaper were initiated and conducted under this legal framework, satisfying the requirement that the interference be prescribed by law.
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued the aim of protecting T.A.’s honour, dignity and professional reputation, as he claimed the article had falsely accused him of criminal misconduct and thereby damaged his public standing (see paragraphs 11 and 14). This falls squarely within the legitimate aim of ‘the protection of the reputation or rights of others’ as recognised under Article 10 § 2 of the Convention.
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: The interference cannot be considered necessary in a democratic society. The article addressed a matter of significant public interest concerning the alleged misuse of public funds by a State-owned company, the Baku Metro, whose chief executive, T.A., was a high-ranking public figure appointed by presidential decree (see paragraphs 5, 6 and 8). The applicant newspaper acted in good faith, basing its criticisms on passenger complaints and its own investigative efforts after the Baku Metro failed to provide explanations about the whereabouts of the remaining card balances (see paragraph 12). As a public figure, T.A. was required to display a greater degree of tolerance towards criticism (see no. 29369/10). Furthermore, the domestic courts failed to conduct a proper balancing exercise: they did not adequately assess the public interest value of the article, the applicant’s status as opposition media, or the disproportionate nature of the Azerbaijan 30,000 damages award, which had a chilling effect on the newspaper’s financial stability and its ability to fulfil its watchdog role (see paragraphs 15, 16, 18 and 19). The ECtHR has consistently held that sanctions for defamation must be proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued and that domestic courts must provide relevant and sufficient reasons for their decisions (see no. 36448/02 and no. 40660/08). In this case, the courts’ reasoning was cursory, and the severe financial penalty imposed was not the least restrictive measure available. Consequently, the interference lacked convincing justification and was not proportionate to the aims pursued.
